questions.prompt: In Chalmers's (2003) taxonomy, how does Type-B physicalism differ from Type-A?

options.text: Type-B denies any epistemic gap; Type-A accepts one
options.why_wrong: The reverse: Type-A denies the epistemic gap.

options.text: Type-B accepts an epistemic gap but denies an ontological one; Type-A denies the gap itself
Type-B expects future science to close the gap; Type-A thinks it never will
Type-B accepts non-physical properties; Type-A does not

questions.explanation: Type-A holds that, on careful reflection, physical knowledge leaves nothing out (zombies are not even conceivable). Type-B grants that physical knowledge does not a priori entail phenomenal truths, but holds that consciousness is physical all the same, with the identities knowable only a posteriori.

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (2003). Consciousness and its place in nature. In S. Stich and T. Warfield (eds.), The Blackwell Guide to Philosophy of Mind. Oxford: Blackwell.

questions.prompt: What is the core claim of the phenomenal concepts strategy?

options.text: Phenomenal concepts refer to non-physical properties
options.why_wrong: That would concede the anti-physicalist conclusion.

options.text: Phenomenal concepts are empty, so qualia do not exist
We have two unlinked ways to pick out one physical state, explaining a gap in understanding without a gap in reality
Phenomenal concepts can be defined in functional terms a priori
options.why_wrong: That is a Type-A claim; the strategy denies an a priori link.

questions.explanation: A third-person neural concept and a first-person phenomenal concept can refer to the same brain state without reasoning alone connecting them, as with 'water' and 'H₂O'. This explains the explanatory gap while keeping physicalism.

sources.citation: Loar, B. (1990). Phenomenal states. Philosophical Perspectives 4, 81-108.
Papineau, D. (2002). Thinking about Consciousness. Oxford University Press.

questions.prompt: What dilemma does Chalmers's 'master argument' (2007) pose for the phenomenal concepts strategy?

options.text: Either phenomenal concepts refer to qualia, or they refer to nothing
options.why_wrong: The dilemma concerns whether the concepts are physically explicable.

options.text: Either phenomenal concepts are physically explicable, so they cannot explain the sense of a gap, or they are not, so physicalism has already failed
Either Mary learns a fact, or she learns an ability
options.why_wrong: That contrasts two replies to the knowledge argument.

options.text: Either zombies are conceivable, or the hard problem is easy
options.why_wrong: This is not the structure of the master argument.

questions.explanation: Chalmers argues that the phenomenal concepts themselves face the same conceivability test: if a zombie could have the same concepts, they cannot explain our epistemic situation; if it could not, the concepts are not physically explicable. Type-B physicalists such as Papineau and Balog reject the dilemma.

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (2007). Phenomenal concepts and the explanatory gap. In T. Alter and S. Walter (eds.), Phenomenal Concepts and Phenomenal Knowledge. Oxford University Press.
Papineau, D. (2002). Thinking about Consciousness. Oxford University Press.

questions.prompt: What does Type-C physicalism hold, and what does Chalmers argue about it?

options.text: That consciousness is fundamental; Chalmers endorses it
options.why_wrong: Type-C is a physicalist view, and Chalmers does not endorse it.

options.text: That the gap is unclosable by humans; Chalmers calls this mysterianism proper
That the gap is purely conceptual; Chalmers calls it the strongest physicalism
That a mature science will close the gap; Chalmers argues it collapses into Type-A or Type-B

questions.explanation: Type-C grants a deep epistemic gap now but expects it to be closable in principle. Chalmers argues that it is unstable: either the gap was never deep (Type-A) or it is only conceptual (Type-B).

sources.citation: Chalmers, D. J. (2003). Consciousness and its place in nature. In S. Stich and T. Warfield (eds.), The Blackwell Guide to Philosophy of Mind. Oxford: Blackwell.
